summary: Describes version 1 of the Sender Policy Framework, which lets a domain say which hosts may send email using its name. It targets forged return paths and forged HELO names. It is an experimental document and was replaced by RFC 7208.

plainLanguage.summary: SPF lets a domain name list, in DNS, the servers that are allowed to send mail pretending to be from it. A receiving mail server looks that list up, compares it with the address of the machine that connected, and reports whether the sender was allowed.

subtitle: How a domain publishes, in DNS, which mail servers may send email using its name, and how receivers check it.

tldr.problem: Any host that injects mail into the mail system can say it comes from any domain it likes, at the level of the session, the envelope and the message headers, which makes it hard to stop spam and harder for domain owners to protect their names.
tldr.mechanism: A domain publishes an SPF record in DNS listing the hosts allowed to send mail using its name. A receiving server looks up that record and evaluates it against the connecting host's address, producing a result such as Pass, Fail or SoftFail that the receiver can act on.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4408 was an Experimental document. It has been obsoleted by RFC 7208 and updated by RFC 6652.

sections.title: Why a Domain Should Say Who May Send Its Mail
sections.content:
The RFC starts with the problem. The current e-mail infrastructure has the property that any host injecting mail into the mail system can identify itself as any domain name it wants. Hosts can do this at a variety of levels, in particular the session, the envelope and the mail headers. Although this feature is desirable in some circumstances, it is a major obstacle to reducing Unsolicited Bulk E-Mail, and many domain name holders are understandably concerned about the ease with which other entities may make use of their domain names, often with malicious intent.

The protocol defined here lets domain owners authorize hosts to use their domain name in the MAIL FROM or HELO identity. Compliant domain holders publish Sender Policy Framework records specifying which hosts are permitted to use their names, and compliant mail receivers use the published records to test the authorization of sending mail transfer agents using a given HELO or MAIL FROM identity during a mail transaction.

There is an additional benefit to receivers. After the use of an identity is verified, local policy decisions about the mail can be made based on the sender's domain rather than the host's IP address, which is advantageous because the reputation of a domain name is likely to be more accurate than the reputation of a host address. And if a claimed identity fails verification, local policy can take stronger action against that mail, such as rejecting it.

The document notes its own status. SPF has been in development since the summer of 2003 and has seen deployment beyond the developers beginning in December 2003. The design slowly evolved until the spring of 2004 and has since stabilized, and the protocol described here is what earlier draft specifications meant by SPF as used in existing implementations, sometimes called SPF Classic.
sections.plainLanguage: Once a receiver has checked the policy, it can judge mail by the domain it claims to be from, which is a more stable thing to judge it by than the sender's address.

sections.title: The Two Identities That Are Checked
sections.content:
Two identities from the SMTP conversation are checked. The HELO identity derives from the SMTP HELO or EHLO command, which identifies the sending host for the session. Requirements for the domain presented in that command are not always clear to the sending party, so SPF clients must be prepared for the HELO identity to be malformed or an IP address literal; at the time of writing, many legitimate e-mails are delivered with invalid HELO domains. It is recommended that clients check the HELO identity separately, by applying the check_host() function to it as the sender.

The MAIL FROM identity derives from the SMTP MAIL command, which supplies the reverse-path for a message. This generally consists of the sender mailbox, and it is the mailbox to which notification messages are to be sent if there are problems delivering the message. The reverse-path may be null, in which case there is no explicit sender mailbox and the message can be assumed to be a notification message from the mail system itself; the MAIL FROM identity is then the mailbox composed of the localpart "postmaster" and the HELO identity. SPF clients must check the MAIL FROM identity, by applying check_host() to it as the sender.

A domain that follows the protocol must publish a valid SPF record authorizing the use of its domain name in the HELO and MAIL FROM identities by the mail servers it specifies. If domain owners choose to publish records, it is recommended that they end in "-all", or redirect to other records that do, so that a definitive determination of authorization can be made. A domain may publish a record that explicitly authorizes no hosts if mail should never originate using that domain. When changing records, care must be taken to ensure there is a transition period, so that the old policy remains valid until all legitimate mail has been checked.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two names in a mail session to check: the one the sending server gives in its greeting, and the one in the envelope. The envelope one is the one that must be checked.

sections.title: The SPF Record
sections.content:
An SPF record is a DNS resource record that declares which hosts are, and are not, authorized to use a domain name for the HELO and MAIL FROM identities. Loosely, the record partitions all hosts into permitted and not-permitted sets, though some hosts might fall into neither category.

The record is a single string of text. The example given in the RFC is v=spf1 +mx a:colo.example.com/28 -all, which has a version of "spf1" and three directives: "+mx", "a:colo.example.com/28", where the plus sign is implied, and "-all".

The record is placed in the DNS tree at the host name it pertains to, not at a subdomain under it, which is different from how SRV records are done. Publishing over TXT records carries a warning: other TXT records published at the same name for other purposes may cause problems with size limits.

The document defines a new DNS resource record of type SPF, code 99, whose format is identical to the TXT record and whose content is encoded as US-ASCII. Using a TXT record is acknowledged as not optimal, but it is necessary because a number of DNS server and resolver implementations in common use cannot handle the new record type. A compliant domain should have records of both types, must have a record of at least one type, and if it has records of both types they must have identical content.

Three further rules apply. A domain must not have multiple records that would cause an authorization check to select more than one record. A single DNS record may be composed of more than one string, and such a record must be treated as if the strings were concatenated together without adding spaces, which is useful for records that exceed the 255-byte maximum length of a string. And the published record should remain small enough that the results of a query for it fit within 512 octets, to keep even older DNS implementations from falling over to TCP; if the combined length of the DNS name and the text of all the records of a given type is under 450 characters, then DNS answers should fit in UDP packets. Records too long to fit in a single UDP packet may be silently ignored by SPF clients.
sections.plainLanguage: The policy is one line of text stored next to the domain name, and it is read by a DNS lookup just like any other name record.

sections.title: The check_host() Function
sections.content:
All of the work is done by one function, check_host(), which takes three arguments: the IP address of the SMTP client emitting the mail, either IPv4 or IPv6; the domain portion of the MAIL FROM or HELO identity; and the MAIL FROM or HELO identity itself as the sender. The domain argument may not be a well-formed domain name, and in those cases check_host() returns None. Implementations must take care to correctly extract the domain from the data given with the SMTP MAIL FROM command, as many mail servers still accept source routes, the %-hack and bang paths, and these archaic features have been maliciously used to bypass security systems.

The function starts by looking up the records for the domain, querying for either the TXT or SPF record type, or both. If all the DNS lookups made return a server failure or another error, or time out, check_host() exits immediately with TempError. Records that do not begin with a version section of exactly "v=spf1" are discarded, and if any records of type SPF are present then all records of type TXT are discarded. After that there should be exactly one record remaining; if there are two or more, check_host() exits immediately with PermError. If no matching records are returned, the client must assume the domain makes no SPF declarations and return None.

The selected record is then parsed and interpreted. Each term is a mechanism or a modifier, and each mechanism may carry a qualifier: "+" for Pass, "-" for Fail, "~" for SoftFail and "?" for Neutral, with the qualifier optional and defaulting to "+". The mechanisms are considered in turn from left to right. When a mechanism matches, processing ends and the qualifier value is returned as the result of the record. When it does not match, processing continues with the next mechanism. When it throws an exception, processing ends and the exception value is returned.

If no mechanism matches and there is no "redirect" modifier, check_host() returns Neutral, exactly as if "?all" had been specified as the last directive. Records should always use either a redirect modifier or an "all" mechanism to terminate processing explicitly.
sections.plainLanguage: The check is a small program that walks the record's terms from left to right. The first term that matches decides the answer; everything after it is ignored.

sections.title: The Mechanisms and Modifiers
sections.content:
There are two kinds of mechanism. Basic mechanisms contribute to the language framework without specifying a particular authorization scheme: they are "all" and "include". Designated sender mechanisms designate a set of IP addresses as permitted or not permitted: "a", "mx", "ptr", "ip4", "ip6" and "exists".

Two conventions apply to all of them. If no CIDR length is given in the directive, the sending address and the address in the mechanism are compared for equality; if a CIDR length is specified, only that many high-order bits are compared. And when a mechanism fetches host addresses to compare, A records are fetched for an IPv4 address and AAAA records for an IPv6 address, so an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address must still be treated as an IPv4 address even when the connection came in over IPv6. A DNS error or timeout makes the mechanism throw TempError, while a "domain does not exist" answer is treated as no error and no answer records.

The all mechanism always matches and is used as the rightmost mechanism to provide an explicit default; mechanisms after it are never tested, and any redirect modifier has no effect when it is present. The include mechanism triggers a recursive evaluation of check_host() against another domain. The RFC is candid that the name was poorly chosen: only the evaluated result of the referenced record is used, rather than the record being treated as literally included, so evaluating a "-all" directive in the referenced record does not terminate the overall processing. A recursive Pass makes include match; Fail, SoftFail and Neutral make it not match; TempError and PermError are thrown; and None raises PermError.

The a mechanism matches if the sending address is one of the target name's IP addresses. The mx mechanism matches if the sending address is one of the mail hosts for a domain name: check_host() performs an MX lookup and then an address lookup on each name returned, and more than 10 MX names must not be looked up during the evaluation of one mx mechanism. The ptr mechanism tests whether the reverse mapping for the sending address exists and correctly points to a domain name within the target domain, looking in in-addr.arpa for IPv4 and ip6.arpa for IPv6, and validating each name by looking up its address in turn; more than 10 PTR names must not be looked up. The RFC discourages the use of ptr because it is slow, is not as reliable as other mechanisms when DNS errors occur, and places a large burden on the arpa name servers.

The ip4 and ip6 mechanisms test whether the sending address falls inside a given network; an omitted CIDR length is taken to be /32 for ip4 and /128 for ip6. The exists mechanism builds an arbitrary domain name and uses it for a DNS A record lookup, which lets a record make fine-grained decisions at the level of the user and the client address; the lookup type is A even when the connection type is IPv6.

The two modifiers are redirect and exp. They always have an equals sign separating the name and the value, may appear anywhere but should appear at the end, and must not appear more than once each, or check_host() exits with PermError. Unrecognized modifiers must be ignored. The redirect modifier applies when all mechanisms fail to match: its domain is expanded and check_host() is evaluated against it with the same address and sender arguments.
sections.plainLanguage: The terms come in two flavours. Some name the servers allowed to send, and some pull in another domain's policy to be judged by.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Processing Limits
sections.content:
The processing limits exist to stop a hostile domain using the check as a denial-of-service weapon. SPF implementations must limit the number of mechanisms and modifiers that do DNS lookups to at most 10 per SPF check, including any lookups caused by "include" or "redirect"; if that number is exceeded, a PermError must be returned. The "all", "ip4" and "ip6" mechanisms require no DNS lookups and do not count, and the "exp" modifier does not count because its lookup happens after the record has been evaluated. When evaluating the mx and ptr mechanisms, or the %{p} macro, there must be a limit of no more than 10 MX or PTR records looked up and checked. Implementations should also limit the total amount of data obtained from the DNS queries, and may impose a limit on the elapsed time to evaluate check_host(); such a limit should allow at least 20 seconds, and if it is exceeded the result should be TempError.

The document then lists four further problems. SPF-authorized mail may contain other false identities: a malicious sender can use his own domain in the identities SPF checks, have that domain's record authorize the sending host, and still list other identities in the message header, so a user may be lulled into a false sense of security. Spoofed DNS and IP data can undermine the check, because an attacker who manipulates the DNS infrastructure can make check_host() return incorrect results, and the client IP address is assumed to be correct, so an attacker who spoofs TCP sequence numbers can make mail appear to come from a permitted host.

Cross-user forgery is not solved by SPF, because SPF policies map domain names to sets of authorized mail servers rather than whole e-mail addresses to sets of authorized users; it is left to mail services and their mail servers to prevent it, for example with SMTP AUTH or message cryptography. Finally, information supplied by third parties, such as the HELO domain name, the MAIL FROM address and the SPF records themselves, is passed to the receiver and possibly returned to the client, so it must be checked for invalid characters and excessively long lines. The explanation string in a rejection may contain malicious URLs, or be offensive or misleading, and both the sender and the receiver need to be aware that the explanation was determined by the publisher of the SPF record and not by the receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: Two limits keep a hostile domain from making the receiver work too hard: at most ten DNS lookups per check, and a cap on how long the check may take.

viz.caption: THE SEVEN RESULTS OF AN SPF CHECK (RFC 4408)

items.label: No policy
items.desc: No records were published by the domain, or no checkable sender domain could be determined.

items.label: No opinion
items.desc: The domain owner explicitly declines to say whether the address is authorized. Treated exactly like None.

items.label: Authorized
items.desc: The client is authorized to inject mail with the given identity.

items.label: Not authorized
items.desc: An explicit statement that the client is not authorized to use the domain.

items.label: Probably not authorized
items.desc: Between Fail and Neutral. Receivers should not reject on this result alone.

items.label: Temporary problem
items.desc: A transient error occurred while performing the check.

items.label: Broken policy
items.desc: The domain's published records could not be correctly interpreted.
